Empirical Research Plan ― “Risk Compensation around Scheduled U.S. Macroeconomic Announcements, 1958-2009”

-----------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
-----------------------------------------------------------
Strategy:  Calendar-based event study implemented as a panel difference-in-differences (DID).

•  “Event study” because the timing of each announcement is known in advance; we estimate average excess returns in very narrow windows around those dates.  
•  “Difference-in-differences” because we compare (i) announcement versus non-announcement days (time dimension) and (ii) across multiple asset classes that differ sharply in ex-ante risk (cross-section).  
•  Exogeneity:  The Bureau of Labor Statistics and the FOMC publish their calendars months ahead; in normal times the exact dates are not moved in response to contemporaneous economic conditions.  Hence the presence of an announcement on a given day can be treated as as-good-as random with respect to unexpected asset-price–relevant shocks.

Why appropriate?  (a) No credible instrument shifts investors’ aggregate risk without also changing their expectations; (b) treatment is sharp and well-timed; (c) daily panel (assets × days) offers >60,000 observations, giving high power.

-----------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control Definitions
-----------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
  Announce_d​t = 1 if day t appears on the pre-announced release calendar for CPI, PPI, Employment Situation, or a *scheduled* FOMC rate decision (1978-2009); 0 otherwise.

Control group  
  All trading days without any of those scheduled macro releases.

Sub-treatments (used for heterogeneity)  
  •  CPI/PPI only  
  •  Employment only  
  •  Scheduled FOMC only  
  •  “High-uncertainty” announcement days = Announce_d​t × top-quintile lagged VIX

Timing / event window  
  Baseline: close-to-close daily returns rᵢt from t−1 to t (the investor must hold the asset over the announcement).  
  Robustness:  (−1,+1) three-day window; intraday 09:30–16:00 window when intraday data are available post-1993.

-----------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
-----------------------------------------------------------
A1.  Conditional exogeneity of release day  
     E[εᵢt | Announce_d​t, X_t ] = 0.  Because the dates are pre-scheduled, any difference in expected returns is attributable to the extra aggregate risk, not contemporaneous shocks.

A2.  No differential pre-trends (parallel trends)  
     In the absence of an announcement, treated and control days would have the same *expected* return path for a given asset after conditioning on day-of-week, month, and year fixed effects.

A3.  No spillovers across days (SUTVA)  
     Expected-return compensation for day t risk does not spill over many days beforehand or afterward; we test this with ±5-day leads/lags.

A4.  No concurrent confounding events systematically aligned with release schedule  
     E.g., triple-witching, FOMC minutes releases, or major holidays; these will be controlled directly or removed.

A5.  Stable asset-class composition  
     Composition changes within CRSP indices are slow relative to daily horizon; any remaining drift is absorbed by asset fixed effects.

Plausibility:  All four agencies set calendars well in advance; only in rare crises are releases postponed (those dates will be dropped).  The first-Friday pattern can be absorbed with day-of-week × calendar-week-of-month dummies, satisfying A2/A4.

-----------------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats and Mitigations
-----------------------------------------------------------
T1.  Calendar seasonality (e.g., first Friday of month)  
     →  Include flexible calendar fixed effects: day-of-week, week-of-month, month-of-year, and year dummies.  Show results unchanged when restricting to a ±10-day window around each employment Friday (within-month event study).

T2.  Overlapping or multiple announcements on same day  
     →  Code mutually exclusive dummies (CPI only, Employment only, etc.).  When overlaps occur (≈6 % of treated days), drop or flag them; show that results hold when overlaps are excluded.

T3.  Anticipatory price drift or information leakage  
     →  Estimate event-time coefficients for k = −5,…,+5.  If k < 0 coefficients are statistically zero, the assumption of no anticipation is validated.

-----------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
-----------------------------------------------------------
```r
library(data.table)
library(fixest)      # fast high-dim FE regressions
library(lubridate)
library(modelsummary)

## 1. Load data  ------------------------------------------------------------
ret   <- fread("daily_asset_returns.csv")      # columns: date, asset, return
ann   <- fread("announcement_calendar.csv")    # columns: date, cpi, ppi, empl, fomc
vix   <- fread("daily_vix.csv")                # columns: date, vix

## 2. Merge & construct variables  -----------------------------------------
ret[, date := as.Date(date)]
ann[, date := as.Date(date)]
vix[, date := as.Date(date)]

dat <- merge(ret, ann, by = "date", all.x = TRUE)
dat <- merge(dat, vix, by = "date", all.x = TRUE)

## Treatment dummies
dat[, announce := (cpi==1 | ppi==1 | empl==1 | fomc==1)]
dat[is.na(announce), announce := 0]

## High-uncertainty interaction (top 20 % lagged VIX)
dat[, lag_vix := shift(vix, 1, type = "lag")]
q80 <- quantile(dat$lag_vix, .80, na.rm = TRUE)
dat[, high_uncert := (lag_vix >= q80)]
dat[, announce_highU := announce * high_uncert]

## Fixed-effect dummies
dat[, dow  := wday(date)]                     # 1 = Sunday … 6 = Friday
dat[, wom  := ceiling(mday(date)/7)]          # week of month 1-5
dat[, month:= month(date)]
dat[, year := year(date)]

## 3.  Main difference-in-differences regression  ---------------------------
# asset FE and rich calendar FE; SEs clustered by date
main_reg <- feols(return ~ announce | asset + dow + wom + month + year,
                  data = dat, cluster = ~date)
etable(main_reg)

## 4.  Heterogeneity by asset class × uncertainty  --------------------------
het_reg <- feols(return ~ announce + announce_highU | asset + dow + wom + month + year,
                 data = dat, cluster = ~date)
etable(het_reg)

## 5.  Event-time leads/lags robustness  ------------------------------------
# Create relative‐event-day index for employment Fridays
empl_dates <- ann[empl==1, date]
window <- 5
leadlag <- rbindlist(lapply(empl_dates, function(d){
   idx <- seq(-window, window)
   data.table(date = d + idx, k = idx)
}))
dat <- merge(dat, leadlag, by = "date", all.x = TRUE)
dat[is.na(k), k := 100]        # 100 = outside window

leadlag_reg <- feols(return ~ i(k, ref=100) | asset + dow + month + year,
                     data = dat, cluster = ~date)
iplot(leadlag_reg)             # visually inspect pre-trends
```

-----------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
-----------------------------------------------------------
Theory (consumption-based CAPM and rare-disaster models) predicts a *positive* risk premium for holding risky assets through aggregate-risk days and a *negative* premium (discount) on near risk-free assets.

•  Equities (value-weighted CRSP): +8 to +12 basis points (bp) excess return on announcement days versus ≈4 bp on non-announcement days.  
•  30-day T-bills: −1 to −3 bp on announcement days.  
•  Long-maturity Treasuries: small +2 bp (they hedge consumption risk poorly when inflation news matters).  
•  Interaction with high VIX: effect magnifies by 50–100 %.

-----------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (1 = satisfied, 0 = questionable)
-----------------------------------------------------------
C1.  Exogenous treatment timing ………………… 1  
C2.  No differential pre-trends ……………………. 1  
C3.  No spillovers / SUTVA ……………………………… 0.5 (possible minor anticipation)  
C4.  No simultaneous confounders ………………. 0.5 (calendar clustering; but controlled)  
C5.  Accurate measurement of treatment …….. 1  

Overall score 4.0 / 5.
